blogs.title: LLMs as Feature Engineers: How FeatLLM Makes Tabular AI Cheaper and Faster
blogs.description: Most LLM-in-tabular tools run the model at inference time for every row. FeatLLM flips the script: it uses an LLM once, up front, to craft rule-based features and then hands prediction off to a tiny downstream model. The result is lower latency, no need for LLM fine-tuning, API-only access, and fewer headaches with prompt length limits.

blogs.title: Designing Prompts that Think: The Two-Step Reasoning Behind FeatLLM
blogs.description: FeatLLM’s prompts mimic an expert analyst. Step 1 extracts general, commonsense relationships between features and the task; Step 2 turns those insights plus few-shot examples into concise, per-class decision rules. With clear instructions and formats, the LLM avoids spurious cues and generates a fixed, useful set of rules that are easy to parse.

blogs.title: From Rules to Ready-to-Train Features: Parsing Natural Language into Code
blogs.description: LLM-generated rules can be messy—symbols swap with words, edge cases creep in. FeatLLM tackles this by asking the LLM to output simple parsing code that converts each rule into a binary feature. This leverages the model’s code understanding, survives minor syntax drift, and produces clean inputs for the downstream classifier.

blogs.title: Do We Still Need Big Models at Inference? Why Simple Linear Heads Win Here
blogs.description: After rules become binary features, FeatLLM trains a lightweight linear model with non-negative weights to estimate class likelihoods. This lets the system learn which rules matter most, outperforming naïve rule counts. It’s fast to train in few-shot settings and keeps inference as light as traditional tabular ML.

blogs.title: Outsmarting Context Limits: Bagging and Ensembles for Scalable Few-Shot Tabular Learning
blogs.description: Long tables can blow past token limits. FeatLLM uses feature and instance bagging to keep prompts small, adds temperature and example reordering for diversity, and ensembles many small rule sets. Self-consistency across trials boosts robustness, while aggregation mitigates occasional bad rules.

blogs.title: Benchmark Breakdown: 13 Datasets, 10% Gains, and 4-Shot vs. 32-Shot
blogs.description: Across diverse tabular tasks, FeatLLM tops or ties state-of-the-art few-shot baselines and averages ~10% gains over alternatives like TabLLM and STUNT. It matches traditional models trained with 32 shots using only 4. Crucially, it keeps inference time low compared with LLM-at-inference methods and remains effective on wide tables.

blogs.title: Fighting Spurious Correlations with Prior Knowledge (and When It Fails)
blogs.description: By explicitly reasoning about feature–label relationships before seeing examples, FeatLLM filters out many irrelevant columns, showing less degradation when noisy features are added. Still, closely related but misleading signals can trip it up—a reminder to review rules and consider domain checks where stakes are high.

blogs.title: A Practitioner’s Guide to Applying FeatLLM: Data Prep, Costs, and Governance
blogs.description: Learn how to go from raw columns to production: write clear task and feature descriptions, craft few-shot examples, generate and parse rules, and train the lightweight head. The post covers API-only setup, budgeting LLM calls, handling privacy, human-in-the-loop rule review, and monitoring drift and bias over time.
